webTitle: Another democratic socialist victory – Angie Nixon in Florida – sends shock waves through party establishment

fields.headline: Another democratic socialist victory – Angie Nixon in Florida – sends shock waves through party establishment
fields.trailText: ‘They call us extreme, they call us radical,’ the progressive Senate candidate said. ‘But I think people see through that’
fields.bodyText: It wasn’t supposed to be this way. In conservative Florida, Alex Vindman – a retired army intelligence officer who blew this whistle on Donald Trump in his first term – appeared set to carry the Democratic establishment banner as the party staged a long-shot bid to topple a Republican US senator. Florida’s Democratic voters had other ideas. Democratic socialist Angie Nixon emerged a surprise victor in the US Senate primary on Tuesday, after a campaign in which she was outfunded and outspent by Vindman at a ratio of more than 10 to one. Her triumph sent shock waves through the Democratic party machine as it prepares to mount a challenge to the incumbent Republican senator, Ashley Moody, in November’s US midterm elections. Nixon, a tenacious leftwing fighter and former union organizer who has represented Jacksonville in the Florida house since 2020, raised $975,000 in her campaign, as against Vindman’s $16.3m, but garnered more than 750,000 votes to her opponent’s 550,000 – an overwhelming victory that left his campaign scratching its head as to where it all went wrong. “The reason that we all collectively thought that he was the favorite was because he had that national name recognition, and especially because he was able to raise so much money,” said Aubrey Jewett, professor of political science at the University of Central Florida. She noted, however, that polling largely focused on how Nixon and Vindman would respectively fare against Moody in a general election, rather than whether Democratic voters preferred Nixon or Vindman as their party’s candidate. “Is Florida ready for a democratic socialist candidate in a general election? I still don’t know the answer,” added Jewett. “But what this primary showed was that, within the Democratic party base, there is a strong majority of progressive social Democrats in Florida – just like there apparently is across the country.” Nixon’s victory followed a series of primary wins for progressive candidates this summer, including in Philadelphia, Colorado, Michigan and New York City. She only recently joined the Democratic Socialists of America, and was not endorsed by them. She is also set to face trial next month – charged with trespassing and resisting an officer without violence – after a sit-in protest at the office of the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, in May. It remains to be seen how attractive Nixon will be to Florida’s wider electorate in November. As Jewett notes, Florida is heavily populated by Hispanic communities, and Moody is certain to try to affix the “socialist” label to Nixon’s campaign that has long proven toxic at the ballot box for such voter groups. The conservative commentator Noah Rothman, writing in National Review on Wednesday, went one step further, characterizing Nixon as “communist-curious”. “Even if the race for Senate in Florida is now a foregone conclusion, this race will still feature prominently in the national conversation,” he argued. “Why? Because it demonstrates that Republicans are right when they warn that the socialist phenomenon is coming to a town near you.” Pollsters already appear to have concluded that Nixon’s primary victory has limited Democrats’ chances of taking the seat. Within hours of her fiery victory speech on Tuesday night, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, the respected analytical wing of the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics, moved the Florida Senate race from “likely Republican” to “safe Republican”. It also leaves Democratic leaders in the US Senate, who publicly warmly welcomed Nixon’s win, in something of a quandary. While their path to reclaiming control of the upper chamber from Republicans was never predicated on success in Florida, Vindman, as a moderate, was considered to have at least an outside shot of an upset. Accordingly, the party’s hierarchy was preparing to send dollars and resources to bolster his campaign. Now, with Nixon on the ticket, analysts expect a rethink. “The Democratic establishment was more comfortable with Vindman,” Jewett said. “He had a demonstrated track record of being able to raise money, and Nixon does not.” Florida has about 1.5 million more registered Republican voters than Democrats, she noted. “Nixon is really going to have her work cut out for her to show that she can raise money, or if she can’t, to show that somehow they can recreate the success of the grassroots campaign that brought her victory here,” Jewett added. Her supporters are certain that will be possible. Among a flood of tributes to her on Tuesday night and through Wednesday were calls for unity, including from Vindman himself, who said: “I will be standing by her side in the fight against Ashley Moody. I hope you’ll join me.” Some of the messages were also critical of Vindman, and those in Democratic circles who bet on the wrong horse. “Angie Nixon’s win sent shock waves through the Democratic establishment who got too comfortable behind corporate donors and moderate candidates,” said Hayley Margolis, an organizer with Jewish Voice for Peace South Florida. “Her votes were hard earned through heartfelt grassroots conversations with the working class across the state of Florida.” Nixon, who was reprimanded for using a bullhorn on the Florida house floor earlier this year, does not care for internal party wrangling. And she made one thing clear: she is unlikely to change tack as she presents herself to the wider statewide electorate before November. “They look at this movement and they call us extreme, they call us radical, but I think people see through that. I won’t let them define me and I know you will always know where I stand,” she told supporters on Tuesday night. “If believing a mom shouldn’t have to work three jobs to keep a roof over her head is extreme, call me extreme. Ashley Moody can call me whatever she wants, but in November she’ll be calling me senator.”

webTitle: Republican senator Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola advance in Alaska Senate primary

fields.headline: Republican senator Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola advance in Alaska Senate primary
fields.trailText: Result tees up marquee race in US midterm elections, which could decide if Republicans or Democrats control Senate
fields.bodyText: Incumbent Dan S Sullivan, the US senator, advanced in Alaska’s non-partisan primary race for his seat on Tuesday alongside Mary Peltola, a former Democratic congresswoman. With the top four candidates moving forward from Alaska’s open primaries to the general election, the Associated Press reported that Sullivan and Peltola had qualified for November’s general election. Another Dan Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher and US Forest Service employee who infuriated his namesake senator by running as a long-shot Republican candidate, was in a distant third place, although his qualification had yet to be confirmed. David B Leslie, a Democrat from Fairbanks, Alaska, is currently in fourth place. He appears to have raised no money for his campaign, and has reportedly said he has no idea why a Super Pac (political action committee) named the American Democracy Project spent about $300,000 supporting his candidacy. After 80% of votes were counted, Peltola led the primary, at 48%, while Sullivan, the senator, had 42.8%. The result tees up one of the marquee races of this year’s US midterm elections, which could determine whether Republicans or Democrats control the Senate for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. First elected in 2014, Sullivan easily won re-election in 2020, but this year faces what is expected to be a stiff challenge from Peltola. She is the first Alaska Native ever to serve in the US House of Representatives, and won a special election for the state’s at-large congressional district in 2022, then a full term later that year. In 2024, Peltola lost her re-election bid to Republican Nick Begich III, but is nonetheless viewed as a top-tier Democratic recruit to take on Sullivan in the Senate race. Both candidates are champions of Alaska’s oil and gas industry – a major employer and economic driver – but Peltola has sought to distinguish herself through her advocacy for the state’s fisheries and opposition to Trump’s economic policies. Sullivan has meanwhile described himself as a reliable advocate both for the state’s oil needs and its military installations, while championing more popular aspects of the president’s agenda such as the tax cut extensions included in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. But Sullivan’s path to retaining his seat in the US Senate has been complicated by the emergence of Dan J Sullivan, his namesake rival, who is also running as a Republican. Alaska Republicans have condemned him as a “sham” candidate who is backed by Democrats and running solely to confuse voters, but their efforts to disqualify him from the race were unsuccessful. Alaska figures prominently in Democrats’ ambitious plans to retake the US Senate, which would require flipping at least three Republican-held seats in states that voted for Trump in 2024. The party is hoping to see its candidates elected in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio and elsewhere, but is also defending seats in Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire. Peltola, who recently replaced her longtime campaign manager, has raised more than $18.5m this election cycle, with upwards of $4.6m on hand. Sullivan has brought in more than $11.7m, with nearly $7.3m on hand. In the primary for Alaska’s sole US House district, Begich advanced to the general election, alongside his main challenger, independent Bill Hill. Alaskans in November will also elect a successor to the incumbent Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, who is barred by term limits from seeking re-election. In a crowded field of 17 candidates, Democrats Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Tom Begich advanced to the November election. Two more nominations remain open, with 80% of votes counted.

webTitle: Unhinged White House response shows senator’s ‘Natalie’ barb struck a nerve

fields.headline: Unhinged White House response shows senator’s ‘Natalie’ barb struck a nerve
fields.trailText: Senator Jon Ossoff, who is up for re-election, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections so far
fields.bodyText: Jon Ossoff really struck a nerve. That much is clear. The US senator for Georgia, running for re-election in November, came up with arguably the standout line of the midterm elections campaign so far when discussing Donald Trump at a rally on Sunday. “While the sailors on the [USS Abraham] Lincoln fight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings. He golfs and trades stocks,” said Ossoff. “See, he doesn’t want to do the job. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.” Not only did the remark enter into national consciousness the existence of “Natalie” – Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old aide to Trump who rarely leaves the president’s side – Ossoff’s riff also succeeded in upsetting Steven Cheung, Trump’s director of communications. “Jon Jackoff,” Cheung wrote on X on Monday, misspelling, perhaps deliberately, the name “Ossoff”, “has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics. Instead of denigrating hard working people serving their country, Jon should look deep into his soul and ask himself why he’s a miserable person who hates this country. It’s because he’s a radical, extremist Dumocrat.” Even for someone in Trump’s orbit, where outbursts against political opponents are commonplace, this plumbed new lows. What could possibly have triggered Trump’s stoutly built, middle-aged communications guru into attacking Ossoff, the handsome, athletic, 39-year-old senator? It’s hard to be sure. But, apropos of nothing, this essay by Dana Schwartz, from 2016, examined why rightwing men are obsessed with calling people “cucks”: “‘Cuck’ is a concept borne [sic] out of insecurity: a fear that one is inadequate, sexually or otherwise, and that inadequacy will lead to the loss of the things that are important to him,” Schwartz wrote. In any case, Trump wasn’t far behind Cheung, calling Ossoff a “Pee-wee Herman lookalike” – a reference to a TV and film character whose popularity peaked 40 years ago. (Trump has also called Ossoff “Pinky Herman”, which is neither a character nor a thing.) The anonymous White House Rapid Response X account joined in too, branding a CNN reporter who had asked Trump about Ossoff a “disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment to her alleged profession”, and later posting: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive. It’s quite troubling.” It’s hard to really be shocked by any of this any more, with daily attacks on the media from the president and his most senior aides, but an official White House account, with 2.2 million followers, invoking a reporter’s children prompted widespread criticism. In truth the rhetoric from Trump and his acolytes, always bellicose, has been getting worse for a while – and people who dare to publicly question Trump’s narrative that he is a successful, popular president, seem to particularly trigger those on the right. Take James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Texas, who is running neck and neck against Ken Paxton, whom Trump picked for the Republican side. Talarico’s popularity in a traditionally red state has seen Republicans come out swinging. Trump dubbed the Democrat “Talafreako” in July; earlier US senator Bernie Moreno had called Talarico, “a far left freak”, while a Texas congressman falsely claiming Talarico “daydreams about trans kids”. (There was also Trump branding a reporter “piggy” after she asked him a question onboard Air Force One.) Perhaps the fury is prompted whenever something, or someone, succeeds in puncturing the alternate reality that Republicans have created for themselves: a reality where the GOP is not predicted to suffer heavy losses in November’s midterms, and one where Trump is a spry, capable president. When someone points out that Trump is an 80-year-old, easily distracted man who is overseeing an ill-defined, meandering war in Iran, while doing little as prices soar at home, it appears to bring out the particularly vulgar insults. Ossoff did all this on Sunday – and sparked fresh speculation about the president’s relationship with a close aide. With Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, stepping down, there is some jostling taking place in Trump’s circle to replace her, perhaps explaining the amped up language as each potential successor seeks to be more pugnacious than the last. And given Democrats in Congress will be running on Trump’s unpopularity this November, there’ll be plenty of opportunity for bellicose responses from the White House. We should brace ourselves for plenty more of this sort of thing.

webTitle: A democratic socialist win and losses for Trump allies: takeaways from primaries in three key states

fields.headline: A democratic socialist win and losses for Trump allies: takeaways from primaries in three key states
fields.trailText: Elections in Florida, Alaska and Wyoming provide a sense of how voters are feeling ahead of November’s midterms
fields.bodyText: Primaries in Florida, Alaska and Wyoming held on Tuesday provided the latest view into how voters are feeling ahead of November’s US midterm elections. One candidate aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) netted an extraordinary win while another was defeated handily. Donald Trump’s handpicked candidates received a mixed reception from voters. In Alaska, voters chose their fighters for one of the year’s marquee US Senate races, and in Florida, extremism remained alive and well among Republicans. Here’s what we learned from the results: Democratic socialists win their first statewide victory In a shocking upset, state representative Angie Nixon beat Alexander Vindman for the Democratic nomination in Florida’s US Senate race, becoming the first member of the DSA to win a statewide primary, although the group did not endorse her. Her odds of victory in November against Republican Ashley Moody appear long, but Nixon’s win was the latest sign that Democratic voters are willing to buck the preferences of their party’s establishment in favor of candidates whose policies and personalities they prefer. Vindman, known for his role as a whistleblower during Trump’s first term, had a significant cash advantage and backing from leading Democrats, yet lost by a wide margin. The US Senate battle is set in Alaska As expected, the Republican senator Dan Sullivan won his primary in Alaska, and former congresswoman Mary Peltola won the Democratic nomination to take him on in what will be one of the top US Senate contests of the year. The state conducts non-partisan primaries in which the top four vote-getters advance, and while counting is not complete, the Associated Press reports that another Republican candidate named Dan Sullivan and Democrat David B Leslie are in the lead to appear on the November ballot. In what may be a troubling sign for Sullivan in the midterms, Peltola led him in the primary, winning 48% of the vote to the Republican senator’s 42.8%. No clear answers for progressives Progressives did not win everywhere. In south Florida, the Democratic congressman Jared Moskowitz won his primary, easily beating DSA-endorsed challenger Oliver Larkin. In the hours that followed, the congressman harshly criticized the DSA and the popular streamer Hasan Piker for campaigning against his renomination, arguing that because his district has been gerrymandered by Florida’s legislature to be more easily winnable for Republicans, he’s the best candidate to keep it in Democrats’ hands in the US midterm elections. Democrats continue to show strength down the ballot A handful of local and special elections offered further evidence that Democratic voters were fired up this year. Pennsylvania statehouse candidate Brandon Dukes won a special election against his Republican opponent Scott Timko, in a seat Trump carried by 18 percentage points in 2024. And though Florida has become increasingly conservative and Republican in the past decade, Democrats ousted a Moms for Liberty board member in Sarasota and won an at-large city council seat in Jacksonville. Extremism in the Republican party was on display The primary elections included several extremist candidates. Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, backed by neo-Nazi influencer Nick Fuentes, lost badly in the Republican primary, but still picked up support in precincts around college campuses. Election denier Chuck Gray won his bid for the at-large US House seat in Wyoming. Congressman Randy Fine, who has been criticized for Islamophobic and homophobic statements, survived a primary challenge from antisemitic and transphobic influencer and businessman Dan Bilzerian. Trump endorsees lose Several candidates Trump had endorsed were not to voters’ tastes. The president had backed state superintendent of public instruction Megan Degenfelder in Wyoming’s Republican gubernatorial primary, but she lost to state senator Eric Barlow. Congressman Cory Mills lost his primary in Florida to former TV reporter Ryan Elijah, while a former official from Trump’s first term, Catalina Lauf, failed in a bid for a nomination to the US House. House GOP solves a problem named Cory Mills Mills’s primary loss is notable also because it solves a problem for House Republicans without dealing further damage to their razor-thin majority. The second-term congressman had been under investigation by the House ethics committee for a range of misconduct, and has faced allegations of domestic assault and fraud. While some House lawmakers had hinted that he should resign, as three other lawmakers facing similar allegations did earlier this year, Mills’s departure could have jeopardized the GOP’s control of the chamber. Instead, two of his Republican colleagues endorsed his successful primary challenger, and Mills’s time in the House will end at the start of next year.

webTitle: Lindsey Graham’s sister and fill-in senator says she’s ‘not that informed on national security’

fields.headline: Lindsey Graham’s sister and fill-in senator says she’s ‘not that informed on national security’
fields.trailText: She made the statement during a debate when asked about potential threats to US national security in South China Sea
fields.bodyText: Asked whether Taiwan and the South China Sea threaten US national security, Republican fill-in senator Darline Graham hesitated. “I’m just going to be honest here,” she told Tuesday night’s debate audience. “I’m – not that informed on national security, so – but I do support the military.” Gasps, and boos, rolled through the opera house hosting the only debate before next week’s Republican runoff – a race to succeed her brother, Lindsey Graham, who was one of the Senate’s most committed rightwing foreign policy hawks before his sudden passing in July. She did not retreat. “I’m not a polished politician up here,” she added. “National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise, but I do support the military.” Her opponent, the ultra-conservative representative Ralph Norman, who once advocated for martial law to keep Joe Biden from the presidency after his election win in 2020, needed no such disclaimer. He walked through Taiwan’s economic ties to the US and made the case that it was worth protecting from Chinese aggression. Graham, endorsed by Donald Trump and leaning on her outsider credentials, recovered later in the evening, describing her family’s reliance on social security survivor benefits after her parents died, and accusing Norman of being unable to decide whether he wants to work in South Carolina or Washington, citing his gubernatorial loss just this year. Norman, who backed his state’s former governor Nikki Haley over Trump in 2024, used the debate to distance himself from the president over the war with Iran, saying Trump “is going to have to tell the American people what it’s going to take” if the strait of Hormuz remains under the control of a country the administration has claimed to have decimated. Since 1979, the US has stuck to what’s called “strategic ambiguity” on Taiwan: refusing to say whether it would actually send troops if China invaded, on the theory that being vague keeps the peace. Trump has largely kept up that dodge, but with his own twist. At his May summit with Xi Jinping in Beijing, the US president said he wasn’t looking to fight a war “9,500 miles” away and wanted “China to cool down”, and put a pending $14bn Taiwan arms package on hold, calling it a “very good negotiating chip”. Xi, meanwhile, told him mishandling the Taiwan issue could lead to “clashes and even conflicts”. Last August, Trump said Xi had personally told him China wouldn’t invade Taiwan while he’s in office – a claim Beijing brushed off, reaffirming its commitment to “reunification”. In South Carolina, early voting begins on Wednesday, ahead of the 25 August primary.

webTitle: Trump is full speed ahead in making money off being the US president | Margaret Sullivan

fields.headline: Trump is full speed ahead in making money off being the US president
fields.trailText: Some restraint on Trump’s excesses might be accomplished if November’s midterm elections give Democrats more power
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump is essentially unrestrained when it comes to enriching himself during his second term, with no sign of stopping. If anything, he’s ramping things up. The numbers so far are astonishing. He amassed $2.2bn in 2025 revenues, the Guardian and other news outlets have reported. And despite widespread criticism of this astonishing fact, very little is standing in the way of his reaping even more. “The Congress has decided not to commit oversight to this topic, and that’s just the fact of the matter at this point,” Eric Lipton, an investigative reporter for the New York Times, told National Public Radio recently. While his actions appall historians, academics and millions of ordinary Americans, they may be within legal boundaries. Moral or ethical boundaries? Not so much. “While Trump’s second term is less than half over, it already looks like the most openly corrupt administration in our history,” Larry Noble, a law professor and former general counsel at the Federal Election Commission, told the Guardian’s Peter Stone. Despite his loyal base of followers, much of the American public isn’t happy about it. Two-thirds of Americans polled by CNN said that this president doesn’t put the good of the United States over his personal gain. His overall approval ratings have tanked to 33% – the lowest level of his presidency – with a disapproval rating at 64%, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll. Startling as the details of his enrichment may be, his mindset – full speed ahead, don’t bother me with past practices – reflects his behavior in other realms. He glories in knowing no restraints or boundaries, and shrugs off criticism. His power is held back only by his “own morality”, he told the New York Times in January. “It’s the only thing that can stop me.” He was speaking specifically about being restrained on the international stage – his freedom to use any military, economic or political power for what he sees as American supremacy. But it’s a mentality he apparently brings into feathering his and his family’s own nest. As Lipton told NPR, queries about apparent conflicts of interest are brushed off, and the party line is that the Trump family’s extracurricular businesses are building the US economy. In earlier presidencies, his actions surely would have political consequences, perhaps impeachment. (He was impeached twice, but not convicted, first in 2019 for abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, then for incitement of the violent insurrection at the US Capitol on 6 January 2021.) Trump has amassed at least $1.4bn last year from his cryptocurrency ventures alone, the Guardian reported, noting that others fared less well; about a million investors in one of his crypto projects suffered nearly $4bn in losses as the value of their holdings cratered. Then there are the wealthy foreigners who have invested in the Trump family’s hotel and golf-resort projects, creating potential conflicts of interest. His media company, Truth Social, has been another major source of wealth. Now there’s a new plan to offer early access to his posts for a fee of $100,000. Those posts, of course, have the power to move markets. It’s come under heavy criticism – and prompted lawsuits from media organizations and advocacy groups such as the Freedom of the Press Foundation that argue it’s unconstitutional. But, to date, as with so much of what Trump does, it’s proceeding brazenly. Every once in a while, the courts step in to provide some restraints. Trump tried to use his already weaponized federal justice department to settle his $10bn lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. The initial result was to provide him and his family immunity from earlier audits of their tax returns, which might save the Trumps about $100m. But in a rare bit of accountability, a federal judge – one appointed by Barack Obama – nullified major parts of the agreement. The legal status is still being contested, and the stakes are high. All of this has the power to shock those paying attention to news reports. But there, too, Trump has given himself a form of protection by constantly playing on citizens’ mistrust of legacy media and to brand such investigations as “fake news”. The result, as author and journalist Craig Unger put it recently on Substack, is that nothing “moves the needle”. Not that long ago, he wrote, the press could “root out corruption, topple presidents, and end wars”. But now, even the biggest scoops and the most dramatic revelations seem to have little impact, Unger argues; that’s because the national citizenry doesn’t share an agreed-upon set of facts as it used to do. Trump’s low approval ratings do seem to tell a different story, however, and voters will get a chance to make their voices heard soon. At the very least, some restraint on Trump’s excesses might be accomplished if November’s midterm elections give Democrats more power with a majority in one or both chambers of Congress. Many forecasters think the Democrats may well regain the House of Representatives but that their getting a majority of Senate seats is quite a bit less likely. For now, Trump continues to take full advantage of a situation that has so greatly benefited his personal wealth, if not his reputation or legacy. Like a greedy toddler, he keeps sticking his hand in the presidential cookie jar. And no one, so far, seems able to yank it out. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

webTitle: Florida primaries: governor matchup set; Democratic socialist shocks establishment-backed nominee in Senate race – as it happened

fields.headline: Florida primaries: governor matchup set; Democratic socialist shocks establishment-backed nominee in Senate race – as it happened
fields.trailText: Trump-backed Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly race to succeed term-limited governor Ron DeSantis; Angie Nixon upsets Alex Vindman in Senate primary
fields.bodyText: Our live coverage is ending now. In the meantime, you can find all of our live US politics coverage here. Millions of voters headed to the polls today for primary elections in Florida, Wyoming and Alaska and a special election to fill former representative Eric Swalwell’s seat in California. We’re still waiting on results from those western states. Byron Donalds won the Republican nomination and David Jolly the Democratic nomination for Florida governor. Donalds was endorsed by Donald Trump and will become Florida’s first Black governor if elected in November. Jolly is a former Republican who joined the Democratic party last year. Progressive Angie Nixon won the Democratic nomination for Florida’s open Senate seat, defeating the heavily favored Alex Vindman, a retired army lieutenant colonel and an impeachment witness against Trump during the president’s first term of office. If elected in November, Nixon would be the state’s first Black senator. Nixon will compete against Republican Ashley Moody in November for the Senate seat Marco Rubio won in 2022. Democratic senator Jon Ossoff called Donald Trump a “draft-dodging, crook president” during a campaign appearance today, continuing a feud with the president that escalated this week. Ossoff is currently running for re-election to his Senate seat in Georgia, and his criticism of the president has received viral attention on social media. The president of the international criminal court (ICC) has been sanctioned by the United States government for its criminal investigation of Israeli officials for crimes committed during its war on Gaza. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, called the ICC “corrupt and fatally politicized” and announced that the US would sanction Tomoko Akane of Japan, the ICC president, and Abdoulaye Seye of Senegal, an ICC senior trial lawyer. Minnesota’s attorney general, Keith Ellison, sued Texas’s governor, Greg Abbott, seeking to compel the extradition of an ICE agent to stand trial for assault and falsely reporting a crime in the wounding of a man during the agency’s immigration crackdown in Minneapolis. The Walt Disney Company, ABC and a number of its affiliated stations filed a federal suit against the Federal Communications Commission on Tuesday to block the government’s demand for an early broadcast license renewal process that the companies describe as motivated by political hostility and an attack on press freedom. Donald Trump posted an image of a map of the strait of Hormuz on his social media platform Truth Social, with a circle around the strait and the words “New US Territory” as the title on Tuesday morning. In a social media post, Alex Vindman said he would back Angie Nixon, after the democratic socialist pulled an unexpected victory over the former army intelligence officer. “Rep Nixon ran a strong campaign. I will be standing by her side,” Vindman wrote. “Who would’ve ever thought that a Jewish refugee would make it to the U.S. Army, to the White House, and to becoming a candidate for the U.S. Senate,” he added. “I still believe in the American Dream, because I’ve lived it.” As we await results in Wyoming and – tomorrow morning – Alaska, here’s more on the key results out of Florida’s primary races: Byron Donalds, a congressman backed by Donald Trump, won the Republican nomination for governor on Tuesday in the race to succeed Ron DeSantis. As my colleague Richard Luscombe reports: “DeSantis did not make an endorsement in the race, but Trump did, backing Donalds and his conservative credentials, with support that could prove decisive in Florida, arguably the heart of Trump’s Make America great again movement, and home to his Mar-a-Lago Palm Beach estate.” And: “In an upset for the Democratic establishment, progressive Angie Nixon won the party’s US Senate primary in Florida, beating former army intelligence officer Alexander Vindman.” Polls have closed in Wyoming, where we’re following key Senate and governor’s races. We’ll bring you the results as the Associated Press calls the races. Florida governor hopefuls Byron Donalds and David Jolly have both addressed supporters following their victories in their respective primaries. Republican nominee Donalds encouraged his party to unite ahead of the general election. “Tonight we put aside our differences. Tonight we are one united Republican party,” he said. Meanwhile, Jolly acknowledged his history as a Republican. “To my Democratic friends, thank you for welcoming me into the party,” he said. Later, he added: “As an old-school Republican, I talk about ending the culture wars not to celebrate some progressive platform, but because I still believe in the old-school Republican, libertarian policy that government should simply stay out of your life.” A few more House primary results are coming in from Florida: Austin Rogers has won the Republican nomination for US House in Florida’s second congressional district. Jimmy Patronis is the Republican nominee in the first district. Scott Singer is the Republican nominee in the 25th district. Jim Schwartzel is the Republican nominee in the 19th district. Seth Harp is the Democratic nominee in the third congressional district. Victor Arias is the Democratic nominee in the 19th district. Kimberly Overman won the Democratic nomination in the 12th district. Robert People won the Democratic nomination in the 15th district. Kelly Kirschner won the Democratic nomination in the 16th district. Ryan Elijah has clinched the Republican nomination for Florida’s seventh congressional district, defeating incumbent Cory Mills, who faced an array of scandals despite receiving Donald Trump’s endorsement in February. Last year, a Florida judge granted a protective order against Mills at the request of his former girlfriend Lindsey Langston, the reigning Miss United States. Mills denies the allegations of domestic violence. Elijah is a former local news anchor. Progressive Angie Nixon has won the Democratic nomination for Florida’s open Senate seat, defeating the heavily favored Alex Vindman, a retired army lieutenant colonel, and an impeachment witness against Trump during the president’s first term of office. If elected in November, Nixon would be the state’s first Black senator. Nixon will compete against Republican Ashley Moody, a former state attorney general, in November. The two are vying to fill the Senate seat Marco Rubio won in 2022. The Associated Press has called the primary results of Florida’s governor’s race: Byron Donalds has won the Republican nomination and David Jolly the Democratic nomination. Donalds, 47, was endorsed by Donald Trump and would become Florida’s first Black governor if elected in November. Jolly, 53, is a former Republican who joined the Democratic party last year. His win in the state’s primary marks the second time in a row that Florida Democrats have nominated a former Republican – following the party’s nomination of former Republican governor Charlie Crist in the state’s 2022 election. Polls have closed across all of Florida as the clock strikes 7pm in the state’s western panhandle region. Pia Dandiya has won the Democratic nomination for Florida’s 22nd congressional district.
